title: Jaw
description: Pathology of the maxilla and mandible — odontogenic and non-odontogenic cysts, jaw tumours, fibro-osseous diseases, deep-space infections, maxillary sinus problems, and dento-alveolar / facial-skeleton fractures.

problems.description: Cheek pain and tenderness over the upper molars, worse on moving the head, with nasal stuffiness on the same side.
problems.etiology:
Usually kicks off after a viral URTI that knocks out cilia activity, leaving the door open for bacterial superinfection — typically a mixed bag of anaerobes, Haemophilus, staphylococci, and streptococci [1]. Less commonly, a foreign body triggers it — roots or water are the classic culprits [1]. Poor drainage through the ostium keeps things festering once they've started [1].

The maxillary antra are the largest of the four paired paranasal sinuses, sitting in each half of the maxilla between the alveolus below, the nasal cavity medially, and the orbits above [2]. The anatomy matters — those close relationships are exactly why upper molar pathology and sinus disease so easily mimic each other.
problems.presentation: Pain and tenderness over the cheeks, nasal discharge or stuffiness, and — the tell — pain that gets worse when the patient moves their head or bends forward [3]. The thing is, antral symptoms mimic maxillary tooth pathology convincingly, so you need to exclude dental causes before calling sinusitis [3]. Head-position-dependent pain is the clue that tips it towards sinus.
problems.results: Occipito-mental X-rays at 15° and 30° can show antral opacity, a fluid level, or a fracture [3]. If you want to define a fluid level properly, repeat the film with the head tilted — it shifts [3]. CT is the tool for tumours, pansinusitis, and blow-out fractures when plain films aren't enough [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Pain that worsens on head movement or bending forward is the key pointer. Diagnosis is effectively by exclusion: dental pathology ruled out, nasal discharge present, cheek tenderness on palpation, and head-position-dependent pain all point here [3]. If you're still unsure, proof puncture settles it [1].
problems.treatment:
Erythromycin 500 mg PO qds or doxycycline 100 mg PO od [1]. Add a decongestant spray — oxymetazoline or xylometazoline [1].

For chronic sinusitis where poor drainage is the problem: remove any foreign body via a canine fossa incision with a bony window into the antrum (Caldwell–Luc), aimed at re-ventilation of the sinus [4].
problems.prognosis: If a foreign body or poor drainage is left untreated, chronic sinusitis develops — mucosal lining hypertrophies and polyps can form [4]. A persistent post-nasal drip is the giveaway in chronic cases [4].

citations.quote: This usually follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection which has ↓ cilia activity, and is due to bacterial superinfection (usually mixed; anaerobes, Haemophilus, staphylococci, and streptococci). Less commonly, due to foreign body (e.g. roots, water). Poor drainage via the ostium exacerbates the situation. ∆ as earlier described and confirmed by proof puncture if necessary. Rx: erythromycin 500mg PO qds or doxycycline 100mg PO od. Decongestants, e.g. oxymetazoline or xylometazoline spray.
These are the largest of the four paired paranasal air sinuses, lying in each half of the maxilla between the alveolus inferiorly, nasal cavity medially, and orbits superiorly.

Often mimics symptoms attributable to maxillary teeth. ∆ is by exclusion of dental pathology, nasal discharge or stuffiness, tenderness over the cheeks, and pain worse on moving the head. Occipito-mental X-rays (15° and 30°) may reveal antral opacity, fluid level, or # (…… Nasal and malar fractures, p. 498). To define fluid level, repeat film with head tilted. Other X-rays: DPT for cysts and roots and CT scans for tumours, pansinusitis, and blow-out #.

Chronic sinusitis may then develop, particularly if a foreign body or poor drainage is present. Mucosal lining hypertrophies and may form polyps. A post-nasal discharge (drip) is often present. Rx: aimed at re-ventilation of the sinus. Foreign bodies, if present, should be removed via an incision in the canine fossa (above the premolars) and creation of a bony window into the antrum (Caldwell–Luc approach).

problems.description: Inability to bring the teeth together after facial trauma, with lingual haematoma, step deformity along the jaw, and possibly numb lower lip.
problems.etiology:
The mandible is the commonest bone to fracture in the facial skeleton [1]. Most result from fights and RTAs [1]. Gunshot wounds are the rare exception — these can be comminuted, with hard and soft tissue loss [1].

Where the fracture lands depends on where the bone is weakest. Condylar neck fractures are the commonest subtype. Angle fractures usually go through the wisdom-tooth socket; body fractures tend to run through the canine socket [2]. So the pattern on imaging often tells you the mechanism.
problems.presentation:
The patient can't bite their teeth together normally [3]. A lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic — if you see it, the diagnosis is made [3]. You'll also find bruising and swelling over the fracture site, bloodstained saliva, and sometimes lacerations [3].

With a displaced fracture, the posterior teeth gag and the mouth hangs open [3]. Ask about lip numbness — paraesthesia in the IDN distribution tells you the nerve is involved [3]. On examination, gentle palpation reveals step deformities, bony crepitus, and tenderness. Trismus is always present to some degree: mouth opening under 40 mm [3].
problems.results: DPT and PA mandible are the essential radiographs [4]. Most trauma-centre patients will also get CT. CT is mandatory before fixing condylar fractures — plain films don't give you the three-dimensional picture you need [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of inability to occlude and a lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic [3]. Palpate the lingual and buccal sulcus for step deformities [5]. If the fracture is subtle and you're unsure, place one hand over each mandibular angle and apply gentle bilateral pressure — even a crack fracture will produce pain [5].
problems.treatment:
Admit. Nurse sitting up, leaning forward [6]. Nil by mouth, IV crystalloid for hydration [6]. Compound fractures need antibiotics [6]. For pain: LA, a temporary bridle wire, parenteral NSAIDs, or opioids as the situation demands [6].

Definitive treatment is ORIF — fracture sites exposed via mucosal incisions, reduced under direct vision, and stabilised with small bone plates and monocortical screws [7].

Condylar fractures over age 12: establish pain-free pre-injury occlusion with elastic traction and reassess at 7 days. If spontaneous pain-free occlusion isn't achieved by then, proceed to ORIF [8].
problems.prognosis: Teeth in the fracture line can often be kept: antibiotics, adequate reduction, and endodontics later as a secondary procedure [7].

citations.quote: These are the commonest # of the facial skeleton (Fig. 12.1). Most are the result of fights and road traffic accidents (the former ubiquitous in Western countries whereas the latter are commoner in the Middle East; the role of alcohol, laws, and attitudes to driving are self-evident). Rarely, they may be comminuted with hard and soft tissue loss, e.g. gunshot wounds.

Condylar neck # are commonest and range from easiest to most difficult. Often found with a # of the angle or canine region of the opposite side of the jaw. Rarely, bilateral condylar # is found with a symphyseal #—'guardsman's #' from falling on the point of the chin. Angle # usually occurs through wisdom-tooth socket, and body # commonly through canine socket.

History of trauma. Ask if the patient can bite their teeth or dentures together in the manner which is normal to them. Inability to do this and a lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic of a mandibular #. Look at the face; there is usually bruising and swelling over the # site and sometimes lacerations. If the # is displaced, there may be gagging on the posterior teeth and the mouth hangs open. The saliva is usually bloodstained. The patient may complain of paraesthesia in the distribution of the IDN. Gentle palpation over the mandible will reveal step deformities, bony crepitus, and tenderness. All have trismus to some degree, opening <40mm.

DPT and PA mandible are the essentials in order to diagnose and assess a mandibular fracture. Most patients in trauma centres will have additional assessment with a CT scan. CT scans are required to assess condylar fractures before fixation.

This may reveal broken teeth or dentures which should be removed. Suction the mouth to clean away blood clots prior to examining both the buccal and lingual sulcus. Look for step deformities in the occlusion, and examine the teeth. Palpate for steps in the lingual and buccal sulcus. If ∆ is uncertain, it is sometimes worth trying to elicit abnormal mobility across the suspected # site, using gentle pressure. In cases where you are very unsure, place one hand over each angle of the mandible and exert gentle pressure; this will produce pain if there is a #, even if it is only a crack #.

Most patients will be admitted to hospital, nursed sitting up and leaning forward as this is the most comfortable position. Keep nil by mouth and maintain hydration by IV crystalloid. Compound # need antibiotics. Assess need for analgesia; LA, temporary immobilization with circumdental wire (bridle wire), parenteral NSAIDs, or opioids may be needed.

# sites are exposed, usually via mucosal incisions, and reduced under direct vision; the teeth are placed in temporary IMF &/or a wire around the tooth on either side of the # (tension band or bridle wire) and small bone plates fixed by monocortical screws are placed to immobilize the reduction.

>12yrs: pain-free, pre-injury occlusion should be established (by elastic traction if need be), and the patient reassessed at 7 days. If spontaneous pain-free occlusion not possible at this stage: ORIF.

problems.description: Fluid or air passing between the mouth and nose after upper molar extraction, with reflux of liquids into the nasal cavity on drinking.
problems.etiology:
What happens is the root removal creates a direct communication between the maxillary antrum and the oral cavity [1]. The anatomy sets this up: the roots of maxillary cheek teeth sit close to the antral floor, so it's easy for roots or even whole teeth to end up in the antrum during extraction, and the alveolar process fractures readily [2].

A fistula is specifically an epithelium-lined tract between the mouth and maxillary sinus [3].
problems.presentation: The patient notices fluid going up into the nose when they drink, or they get minor nosebleeds after the extraction [3]. Confirm it by asking them to attempt to blow out against a closed nose — air bubbles through the socket [3]. Occasionally you'll see antral mucosa prolapsing through the socket itself [3].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis, confirmed by the closed-nose blow test [3]. Occipito-mental views or DPT can show antral mucosal changes or a retained root sitting up in the sinus [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: An epithelium-lined tract between mouth and maxillary sinus [3]. Almost always follows extraction of an isolated molar — the single-tooth socket is the vulnerable site [3]. The tendency to persist is what separates a fistula from a simple post-extraction communication that closes within a few days [3].
problems.treatment:
Diagnosed at the time of extraction: close the socket by suture or buccal advancement flap, prescribe antibiotics and decongestants as for maxillary sinusitis, and tell the patient not to blow their nose [3].

Diagnosed more than 2 days after extraction: start antibiotics and decongestants for 2 weeks, then review at 6 weeks [3].

Buccal advancement flap: excise the fistula to create a clean line of closure over bone, raise a broad-based full-thickness buccal flap, incise the periosteum so the mucosa can stretch over the socket, and close with vertical mattress sutures over bone [5]. Alternatives are a palatal rotation flap based on the palatine artery [6] or a buccal fat pad flap [7]. Decongestant: ephedrine nasal drops 0.5–1%, 1–2 drops into the relevant nostril qds for 7–10 days [8]. Refer to oral surgery if you can't close it yourself [1].
problems.prognosis: Many small fistulae are asymptomatic and close without treatment [3]. Persistent ones need surgical closure — the buccal advancement flap is reliable but does reduce sulcus depth [5].

citations.quote: This is a complication that can occur during root removal, whereby a communication between the maxillary antrum and the oral cavity is created. If the root is removed, then the operator should close the communication with local full-depth mucoperiosteal flaps. If not able to carry out this procedure, a referral should be made to the local oral surgery department. The patient should be encouraged to avoid blowing their nose until resolved and a nasal decongestant prescribed (0.5% ephedrine nasal drops for 5 days).

The proximity of maxillary cheek teeth to the antral floor makes it easy for roots and even teeth to be displaced into the antrum. It also predisposes to # of the alveolar process during 6, 7, 8 extraction.

This is the creation of a pathological epithelium-lined tract between the mouth and maxillary sinus. This most often occurs following the extraction of isolated molar teeth when the fistula tends to persist. Post-extraction reflux of fluids into the nose or minor nosebleeds are diagnostic pointers. Confirm by getting the patient to attempt to blow out against a closed nose; air bubbles through the fistula. Occasionally, antral mucosa prolapses through the socket. Rx: many small fistulae are asymptomatic and close spontaneously. Closure if ∆ is made at the time of extraction: close the socket by suture or buccal advancement flap (Fig. 10.13), give antibiotics and decongestants as for maxillary sinusitis, and advise not to blow the nose. Closure if ∆ is made >2 days after extraction: place on antibiotics, etc., for 2 weeks and review after 6 weeks.

Often mimics symptoms attributable to maxillary teeth. ∆ is by exclusion of dental pathology, nasal discharge or stuffiness, tenderness over the cheeks, and pain worse on moving the head. Occipito-mental X-rays (15° and 30°) may reveal antral opacity, fluid level, or #. To define fluid level, repeat film with head tilted. Other X-rays: DPT for cysts and roots and CT scans for tumours, pansinusitis, and blow-out #.

Buccal advancement flap—excise fistula to prepare a line of closure over bone and raise a broad-based buccal flap. Incise periosteum to allow mucosa to stretch over the socket and close, over bone, with vertical mattress sutures. Use antibiotics, etc., remove sutures at 10 days. Disadvantages: thin tissue may break down; reduces sulcus depth.

Palatal rotation flap—excise fistula as for buccal advancement flap. Dissect a palatal mucoperiosteal flap based on palatine artery, rotate over socket, and suture in similar fashion (Fig. 10.14). Disadvantages: bare bone left to granulate; difficult flap to rotate without distortion.

Buccal fat pad flap—if after raising the buccal advancement flap the periosteal incision is opened with artery forceps, the buccal fat pad is exposed. This can be easily mobilized as a pedicled flap to suture into and obtund the defect.

Dose: ephedrine nasal drops 0.5–1%, 1–2 drops into the relevant nostril qds for 7–10 days. For symptomatic nasal decongestion and as an adjunct to the management of oro-antral fistulae inhalation of menthol and eucalyptus is valuable.

problems.description: Painless buccal expansion of the jaw around an unerupted tooth found on routine X-ray, with delayed eruption of the associated permanent tooth.
problems.etiology: Forms around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth — the cyst wall arises from the reduced enamel epithelium that normally sits over the crown [1]. The interesting bit is that it can interfere with eruption: the cyst physically blocks the tooth's path, so eruption is delayed or fails altogether [1].
problems.presentation: Often picked up incidentally on a routine X-ray before the patient notices anything. When symptomatic, you get a painless swelling causing buccal expansion of the jaw, and the associated tooth is missing from the arch or delayed [1].
problems.results: Radiolucent area enveloping the crown of an unerupted tooth. Always submit the cyst lining for histopathology — you need to confirm what you're dealing with [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Specifically arises from reduced enamel epithelium around an unerupted permanent tooth's crown [1]. That's what distinguishes it from a radicular cyst, which arises from a necrotic pulp [3]. The rule of thumb: dentigerous cyst = unerupted tooth; radicular cyst = dead tooth.
problems.treatment: Two options depending on what you want to do with the tooth. Enucleation removes the cyst cleanly and the tooth with it [1]. Marsupialization opens the cyst into the mouth — it's slower to heal and leaves a cavity for a while, but it allows the tooth to erupt through if that's the goal [4]. Always send the lining for histopathology [2].
problems.prognosis: Enucleation is curative. Marsupialization is slower but gives the tooth a chance — so the choice comes down to whether preserving that tooth is worth the longer healing time [4].

citations.quote: These form around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth and arise from reduced enamel epithelium. May delay eruption. Rx: marsupialization or enucleation, depending on position and desired fate of the tooth.
Always submit cyst lining for histopathology.

These are very common, and may also be called radicular cysts. Described as apical or lateral depending on position in relation to tooth root, or residual if left behind after tooth extraction. Necrotic pulp is the stimulus, and the epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez.

Marsupialization. This is the opening of the cyst to allow continuity with the oral mucosa; healing is slower than with enucleation and a cavity persists for some time. It is useful to allow tooth eruption through the cyst or where enucleation is C/I.

problems.description: Slowly expanding swelling of the posterior lower jaw, more common in men and those of African descent, expanding the cortex rather than perforating it.
problems.etiology:
One of the more common odontogenic tumours — so while it's uncommon in absolute terms, it's the one to know [1]. Seen most often in men and in people of African descent, and it has a strong predilection for the posterior mandible [1].

Three subtypes, and the distinction matters for management. Unicystic is the least aggressive — it expands bone without invading it. Polycystic and peripheral types invade surrounding tissue [1]. So when you see it on imaging, the pattern of bone involvement already tells you something about behaviour. Metastases are very rare [1].
problems.presentation: Slow-growing, painless expansion of the posterior mandible. The unicystic type pushes the cortex out; the polycystic and peripheral types eat into surrounding tissue [1]. Histologically you'll see either a plexiform or follicular pattern — though that distinction is the pathologist's problem, not yours at the chair [1].
problems.results: Radiolucent lesion on X-ray. The multiloculated appearance can look identical to a keratocyst [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Posterior mandible, men, African descent [1]. Three subtypes with very different aggression levels: unicystic expands, polycystic and peripheral invade [1]. Metastases are very rare but do occur [1]. The question is always: which subtype? — because that determines the margin you need.
problems.treatment: Unicystic: enucleation, but you must also remove a rim of the enclosing bone [1]. Polycystic and peripheral: excision with a margin — these types invade, so clean edges matter [1].
problems.prognosis: Unicystic type has a low recurrence risk after enucleation with a rim of bone [1]. Polycystic and peripheral types carry a higher recurrence risk because of tissue invasion — incomplete excision will bring it back [1]. Metastases are very rare [1].

citations.quote: One of the commoner odontogenic tumours. Commonest in men and Africans, and in the posterior mandible. There are three basic types: unicystic, polycystic, and peripheral. The unicystic type is the least aggressive; the polycystic and peripheral types show a tendency to invade surrounding tissue, whereas the unicystic expands it. Metastases are very rare. Histologically, two types are seen: plexiform and follicular. Rx: unicystic can be enucleated provided a rim of enclosing bone is removed as well; the other types require excision with a margin.
Their multiloculated appearance on X-ray may confuse them with an ameloblastoma.

problems.description: Exposed, non-healing jaw bone in a patient taking anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication, often following a tooth extraction.
problems.etiology:
Several anti-resorptive and anti-angiogenic drugs have been linked to MRONJ, but bisphosphonates are the most common culprit [1]. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast function [2]. They're not all equal: non-nitrogen-containing oral preparations are the least potent; nitrogen-containing IV preparations are the most potent [3].

Denosumab — a human monoclonal antibody that blocks osteoclast formation, function, and survival — and anti-angiogenic drugs like bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept carry the same risk [4]. The underlying principle is simple: any surgery that requires osteoclast activity for healing is unsafe in a patient on these drugs [1].
problems.presentation: Exposed alveolar bone in the mouth in a patient on anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication [5]. May be painful or painless. Non-healing extraction socket is the classic trigger, but bone necrosis without any mucosal breach is also described [5].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis: exposed necrotic jaw bone in someone on the relevant drugs [5]. The condition appears progressive, and there is no established effective treatment [5]. So what you're dealing with is not a problem you fix — it's a problem you prevent.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Exposed alveolar bone linked to anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic drug use [5]. Usually follows extraction or dento-alveolar surgery, but not always [5]. The incidence range is stark: less than 1% for low-potency drugs used in osteoporosis, up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10 years who've had extractions and highly potent drugs [5]. That spread is why risk assessment matters — the conversation with a post-menopausal woman on alendronate is very different from the one with a myeloma patient on zoledronate.
problems.treatment:
The goal is to avoid surgery requiring osteoclast activity for healing [1]. If you can manage a tooth endodontically or via coronectomy instead of extracting it, do that.

If extraction is unavoidable: warn the patient of the risk (range <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10 years). Then: prophylactic chlorhexidine, broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone sits well below the gingival margin, and primary mucosal closure [6].

For established MRONJ: limited sequestrectomy with coverage of the exposed bone. Refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery [7].
problems.prognosis: No agreed effective treatments for established MRONJ exist [7]. Tactics that work for osteoradionecrosis don't seem to help here [7]. Prevention is the most useful thing you can do — ideally, all patients should have optimal dental health before starting bisphosphonates, making future extractions unlikely [8].

citations.quote: Several anti-resorptive and anti-angiogenic drugs that are prescribed in the UK have been associated with MRONJ but commonly it is due to bisphosphonates. Risk assessment is required and the Rx needs to be tailored according to the risk. The principle is not to carry out any surgery which requires osteoclast activity for healing on someone taking these drugs.

Bisphosphonates constitute a wide group of agents which act primarily by inhibiting osteoclast function which helps prevent fractures in osteoporosis, stabilizes Paget's disease, relieves bone pain and fractures in bone metastases in a range of malignancies, and can treat hypercalcaemia of carcinomatosis. Unfortunately, one of their side effects is necrosis of jaw bone, usually (although not always) associated with extractions or dento-alveolar surgery.

They come in differing degrees of potency, non-nitrogen-containing oral preparations being the least potent and nitrogen-containing IV preparations being the most potent. Osteoporosis tends to be managed with less potent drugs and hypercalcaemia and bone metastases with the most.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast formation, function, and survival. It is used in the treatment of osteoporosis, bone metastasis, and a number of other conditions that result in ↑ bone turnover. It is only available in IV form and is considered a million times more potent than etidronate. Denosumab and other non-bisphosphonate drugs such as anti-angiogenic drugs bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept still have the potential to cause bone necrosis. This is known as 'medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw' or 'MRONJ'.

Bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (BRONJ aka BRON aka anti-resorptive-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (ARONJ)) is a condition where alveolar bone is exposed in the mouth in patients taking these drugs. The condition appears to be progressive and there is no established effective treatment although several are being investigated. Bone necrosis without mucosal breach is also described. The incidence is variable but is probably much less than 1% for patients treated with low-potency drugs for osteoporosis, up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10yrs who have received highly potent drugs and who have had extractions.

If this can be avoided by endodontics, coronectomy, etc. then do it. If not, warn the patient of risks (range from <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis patient to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10yrs). Use prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, and alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone lies well below the gingival margin and close mucosa primarily.

There are no agreed effective Rxs to date. Tactics that work for osteoradionecrosis do not seem to help. Limited sequestrectomy coupled with some form of coverage of the exposed bone seems to help and a variety of supplemental drug Rxs are being used but there is no established evidence base for this. Refer to your local oral and maxillofacial surgery department.

Prevention is the most useful management strategy and all patients prior to starting bisphosphonates should have optimum dental health established such that it is highly unlikely they will ever need to have a tooth removed in the future.
